source_batch.unit_label: ABFM Module B unit 3 (courseware unit 9): capital investment decisions

facts.statement: Objective of capital investment decisions (courseware): the goal of management is to maximise the wealth of shareholders; the finance manager identifies investment opportunities that raise the value of the company. A company that does not invest even in replacing ageing plant will shrink; one that passes up valuable opportunities misses chances; one that invests in every opportunity returning more than shareholders could earn themselves increases owners' wealth. The decision first assesses the requirement and then the sources, cost, form and time schedule.

Estimating project cash flows (courseware): a project has three elements of cash flow: initial (capital expenditure and net working capital), operating (inflows and outflows from operations) and terminal (what remains on liquidation at the end of the economic life). Four principles: the separation principle (separate the investment side from the financing side, so interest is not in the investment cash flows); the incremental principle (count only the costs that would not arise without the project); the post-tax principle (use after-tax cash flows, since tax cannot be ignored); and the consistency principle (use a discount rate consistent with the cash flows). Cash inflow after tax (CFAT) = sales less variable cost = contribution; less fixed cash cost and depreciation = earnings before tax; less tax = earnings after tax; add back depreciation = cash inflow after tax. Worked example: depreciable base Rs 1,00,000 over 4 years gives depreciation of Rs 25,000 a year.

Project cost (courseware): the cost of a project is the investment in fixed assets (land, building, plant and machinery, electrical and power lines, environment protection equipment, and intangible assets such as registrations and patents) together with installation cost, direct costs of setting up and other pre-operative costs, which are capitalised to the assets. The analysis of the total cost examines: necessity, the best combination, competitive bargaining, cost versus recoverable duties (input tax credit is not part of cost to the extent it is recoverable), leveraging (buy or lease), the life span of the assets (too long means high repair cost and outdated technology, too short means frequent replacement), justification, environmental impact, growth considerations, sustainability and the returns projected.

Payback period (courseware): the payback period is the period in which the initial investment is fully recovered from net cash inflows. When annual inflow is the same it equals the amount initially invested divided by the annual net cash inflow; when inflows differ, cumulative inflows are added until they equal the investment, with the fraction of the final year taken as balance needed divided by that year's inflow. Properties: simple; suitable for small businesses; ignores the time value of money unless discounted; ignores cash flows after the payback period; a shorter payback means less risk. Cash inflow equals profit after tax plus depreciation. The discounted payback period uses discounted cash flows. Worked example: Rs 2,00,000 outlay and inflows of 80,000, 60,000, 60,000 and 20,000 recover the outlay in 3 years; for an outlay of Rs 2,05,000 the payback is 3.25 years.

Accounting rate of return (courseware): ARR is average annual net income (profit after tax and depreciation) divided by investment, expressed as a percentage; it uses accounting information, is easy and familiar, but is profit-centric, ignores the time value of money and mixes a numerator belonging to owners with a denominator of total investment. Versions: on the investment at the beginning (initial investment); or on the average investment, where average investment = half of (initial investment less salvage value) plus salvage value. Worked example: Rs 3,00,000 investment, salvage Rs 90,000, annual profit after depreciation Rs 80,000 gives 26.67 per cent on the initial investment and 41.03 per cent on the average investment of Rs 1,95,000. The method can show the same ARR for projects with different timing of benefits.

Net present value (courseware): NPV is the present value of net cash inflows less the net initial investment, with future flows discounted at the required rate; a rupee now is worth more than a rupee later. Decision: accept if NPV is positive; if NPV is zero the project neither adds nor loses value; negative is a red signal; among mutually exclusive projects choose the higher NPV. Strengths: it recognises the time value of money and the surplus created. Limits: the discount rate is subjective and estimates are uncertain. Working capital: an increase is an outflow and a decrease an inflow. Capital rationing means a limit on funds, handled by norms such as a higher IRR or profitability index. Equivalent annual cost (EAC) is the annual cost of owning and operating an asset over its life and compares assets with different lives. Worked example: investment Rs 1,00,000; inflows of 55,000, 80,000 and 15,000 at 10 per cent with factors 0.909, 0.826 and 0.751 give discounted inflows of 49,995, 66,080 and 11,265, totalling 1,27,340, so NPV is Rs 27,340.

IRR and MIRR (courseware): the internal rate of return is the discount rate that sets NPV to zero; it is found by trial and error and interpolation (NPV at the lower rate divided by the sum of the absolute NPVs at the two rates, added to the lower rate); accept if IRR is greater than the cost of capital (required rate of return), reject if less. Limits: unreliable if cash flows are hard to predict, and unconventional cash flows (alternating signs) can give multiple IRRs. IRR assumes intermediate inflows are reinvested at the IRR itself. MIRR corrects this: the present value of costs (PVC) is found at the cost of capital; the terminal value (TV) of inflows is compounded at the cost of capital to the end of the project; MIRR solves PVC = TV / (1 + MIRR)^n, giving one value. Both IRR and MIRR may mislead when ranking projects of different sizes. Worked example (Square Limited): cost of capital 15 per cent; PVC 379.13, TV 934.07, six years, so MIRR is 16.2 per cent and the project is acceptable.

Profitability index and social cost benefit analysis (courseware): the profitability index (PI) = sum of discounted cash inflows / initial cash outlay (or total discounted outflow); a PI above 1 is profitable and below 1 unprofitable; a higher index is better, and PI helps rank projects (for example PI of 1.18, 1.27 and 1.001 for three projects, although the third gives the highest absolute inflow). Social cost benefit analysis (SCBA) is used for public infrastructure projects by governments and local bodies: it values social costs (pollution, loss of mangroves, health hazards) as negative and benefits (travel and time savings, employment, improved living standards) as positive; if the net result is positive and at least equal to the project cost, the project is considered beneficial. Courseware summary: none of payback, discounted payback, NPV, PI, IRR and MIRR considers all cash flows, timing and risk, nor does any maximise owners' wealth by itself.

payload.title: Why firms make capital investment decisions
payload.core_explanation_md:
The goal is to **maximise shareholders' wealth**. A firm that **never invests**, not even to replace worn plant, **shrinks**. One that **skips good opportunities** loses wealth. One that **invests in every project returning more than shareholders could earn elsewhere** **increases wealth**.

The decision first asks **how much is needed**, then the **source, cost, form and timing** of funds.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware contrasts three companies with identical opportunities but different investment policies.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Those whose return exceeds what the shareholders could have earned themselves.

payload.title: Estimating project cash flows
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Three elements:** **initial** (capital expenditure and net working capital), **operating** (yearly inflows and outflows) and **terminal** (what remains at the end of life).

**Four principles:** **separation** (keep financing flows such as interest out of the investment flows), **incremental** (count only costs that arise **because of** the project), **post-tax** (use **after-tax** flows) and **consistency** (a discount rate consistent with the flows).

**CFAT:** sales less variable cost, less fixed cash cost and depreciation = **EBT**; less tax = **EAT**; **add back depreciation** = **cash inflow after tax**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Depreciation is deducted to find tax but added back because it is not a cash outflow.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is depreciation added back to earnings after tax?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because it is a non-cash charge; it only reduces tax.

payload.title: Project cost and what to test in it
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Project cost** includes **fixed assets** (land, building, plant, power lines, environment equipment, intangible assets), **installation**, **direct costs of setting up** and other **pre-operative costs**, capitalised to the assets.

**Tests applied:** **necessity**, **best combination**, **competitive bargaining**, **recoverable duties** (input tax credit is **not** part of cost where recoverable), **buy or lease**, **asset life**, **justification**, **environmental impact**, **growth** and **sustainability**, and the **projected returns**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A very long life means high repair cost and old technology; a very short life means frequent replacement.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is recoverable input tax credit excluded from asset cost?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the tax is offset against duties collected, so it is not a real cost.

payload.title: Payback period
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Payback period = investment / annual net cash inflow** when inflows are **equal**.

When inflows **differ**, add **cumulative** inflows year by year until they equal the investment; the part of the last year is **balance still to recover / that year's inflow**.

**Cash inflow = profit after tax + depreciation.**

Payback is **simple** and shows **risk** (shorter is safer), but it **ignores the time value of money** and **all flows after payback**. The **discounted payback** uses **present values**.

assumptions: Inflow accrues evenly in the final year
common_errors: Using profit instead of cash inflow
Forgetting the fraction of the final year

payload.expanded_explanation_md: With unequal flows, a payback of 3.25 years means the first three years recover all but the last quarter of the fourth year.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The time value of money and all cash flows after the payback period.

payload.title: Accounting rate of return
payload.core_explanation_md:
**ARR = average annual profit after tax and depreciation / investment x 100.**

**Two bases for investment:** the **initial investment**, or the **average investment = half of (initial investment - salvage value) + salvage value**.

ARR uses **accounting profit** (not cash flow) and **ignores the time value of money**, so two projects with the **same ARR** but different timing of benefits look alike.

common_errors: Using cash inflow instead of profit
Using initial investment when average investment is required

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware notes an internal inconsistency: the numerator belongs to owners while the denominator is total investment.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Half of (initial investment less salvage value) plus salvage value.

payload.title: Net present value
payload.core_explanation_md:
**NPV = present value of net cash inflows - initial investment**, discounting each year's flow at the **required rate**.

**Decision:** **accept if NPV is positive**; **zero** means the project neither adds nor loses value; **negative** means reject. Among **mutually exclusive** projects, take the **higher NPV**.

**Working capital:** an **increase** is an **outflow**, a **decrease** an **inflow**. **EAC** compares assets with **different lives**.

variables.name: Net cash inflow in year t
Required rate of return (cost of capital)

assumptions: Cash flows occur at year ends
The discount rate is known and constant

payload.expanded_explanation_md: NPV is the amount by which the value of the business rises if the project is undertaken.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a zero NPV mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The project earns exactly the required rate, adding neither value nor loss.

payload.title: IRR and MIRR
payload.core_explanation_md:
**IRR** is the discount rate at which **NPV = 0**. Find it by **trial and error**, then **interpolate**: lower rate + (NPV at lower rate / (NPV at lower + absolute NPV at higher)) x the gap between the rates. **Accept if IRR exceeds the cost of capital.**

**Limits:** **multiple IRRs** with **alternating cash flows**, and the assumption that inflows are **reinvested at the IRR**.

**MIRR** fixes this: **PVC** = present value of costs at the cost of capital; **TV** = inflows compounded to the end at the cost of capital; **MIRR solves PVC = TV / (1 + MIRR)^n**, giving **one** answer.

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Both IRR and MIRR can mislead when ranking projects of different sizes, because a larger project with a lower rate can have the higher NPV.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can IRR give multiple answers?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When cash flows change sign more than once, the NPV equation can have several roots.

payload.title: Profitability index and capital rationing
payload.core_explanation_md:
**PI = sum of discounted cash inflows / initial cash outlay.**

**PI above 1** means profitable; **below 1** unprofitable. A **higher PI** ranks higher, even where another project has **larger absolute inflows**, because PI is **per rupee invested**.

**Capital rationing** limits the funds available; firms respond with norms such as a **higher IRR or PI hurdle**.

assumptions: Same discount rate for all projects
common_errors: Using NPV instead of present value of inflows in the numerator

payload.expanded_explanation_md: PI above 1 is equivalent to a positive NPV for a given project.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can a project with the largest inflows have a low PI?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because its outlay is also very large, so inflow per rupee invested is low.

payload.title: Social cost benefit analysis
payload.core_explanation_md:
**SCBA** is used by **governments and local bodies** for **infrastructure** such as airports, ports and dams.

It gives **negative** value to **social costs** (pollution, loss of mangroves, health hazards) and **positive** value to **social benefits** (time and fuel savings, employment, better living standards).

The project is **beneficial** if the **net social result is positive** and at least equal to the project cost.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Unlike private appraisal, it counts costs and benefits to society, not only cash flows to the owner.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two social costs and two social benefits.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Costs: pollution and loss of mangroves. Benefits: time savings and employment.

payload.stem_md: A project costs Rs 4,00,000 and gives net cash inflows of Rs 1,60,000, Rs 1,60,000, Rs 1,20,000 and Rs 80,000 in years 1 to 4. What is the payback period (years, to 2 decimal places)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Cumulative inflows are 1,60,000 after year 1 and 3,20,000 after year 2, leaving 80,000 to recover. In year 3 the inflow is 1,20,000, so the fraction is 80,000 / 1,20,000 = 0.67. Payback is 2.67 years.

payload.stem_md: A project costing Rs 12,00,000 gives equal annual net cash inflows of Rs 2,50,000. What is the payback period (years, to 1 decimal place)?

A new product line has annual sales of Rs 10,00,000, variable cost of Rs 5,50,000, fixed cash cost of Rs 1,00,000 and depreciation of Rs 1,50,000. The tax rate is 30 per cent. What is the cash inflow after tax (Rs)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Contribution = 10,00,000 - 5,50,000 = 4,50,000. EBT = 4,50,000 - 1,00,000 - 1,50,000 = 2,00,000. Tax at 30 per cent = 60,000, so EAT = 1,40,000. Adding back depreciation of 1,50,000 gives CFAT of Rs 2,90,000.

For the same machine, what is the ARR on the initial investment (per cent, to 1 decimal place)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: ARR on the initial investment = 80,000 / 6,00,000 = 13.3 per cent.

items.title: Why firms make capital investment decisions
items.core_explanation_md:
The goal is to **maximise shareholders' wealth**. A firm that **never invests**, not even to replace worn plant, **shrinks**. One that **skips good opportunities** loses wealth. One that **invests in every project returning more than shareholders could earn elsewhere** **increases wealth**.

The decision first asks **how much is needed**, then the **source, cost, form and timing** of funds.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware contrasts three companies with identical opportunities but different investment policies.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Those whose return exceeds what the shareholders could have earned themselves.

items.title: Estimating project cash flows
items.core_explanation_md:
**Three elements:** **initial** (capital expenditure and net working capital), **operating** (yearly inflows and outflows) and **terminal** (what remains at the end of life).

**Four principles:** **separation** (keep financing flows such as interest out of the investment flows), **incremental** (count only costs that arise **because of** the project), **post-tax** (use **after-tax** flows) and **consistency** (a discount rate consistent with the flows).

**CFAT:** sales less variable cost, less fixed cash cost and depreciation = **EBT**; less tax = **EAT**; **add back depreciation** = **cash inflow after tax**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Depreciation is deducted to find tax but added back because it is not a cash outflow.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is depreciation added back to earnings after tax?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because it is a non-cash charge; it only reduces tax.

items.title: Project cost and what to test in it
items.core_explanation_md:
**Project cost** includes **fixed assets** (land, building, plant, power lines, environment equipment, intangible assets), **installation**, **direct costs of setting up** and other **pre-operative costs**, capitalised to the assets.

**Tests applied:** **necessity**, **best combination**, **competitive bargaining**, **recoverable duties** (input tax credit is **not** part of cost where recoverable), **buy or lease**, **asset life**, **justification**, **environmental impact**, **growth** and **sustainability**, and the **projected returns**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A very long life means high repair cost and old technology; a very short life means frequent replacement.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is recoverable input tax credit excluded from asset cost?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the tax is offset against duties collected, so it is not a real cost.

items.title: Payback period
items.core_explanation_md:
**Payback period = investment / annual net cash inflow** when inflows are **equal**.

When inflows **differ**, add **cumulative** inflows year by year until they equal the investment; the part of the last year is **balance still to recover / that year's inflow**.

**Cash inflow = profit after tax + depreciation.**

Payback is **simple** and shows **risk** (shorter is safer), but it **ignores the time value of money** and **all flows after payback**. The **discounted payback** uses **present values**.

assumptions: Inflow accrues evenly in the final year
common_errors: Using profit instead of cash inflow
Forgetting the fraction of the final year

items.expanded_explanation_md: With unequal flows, a payback of 3.25 years means the first three years recover all but the last quarter of the fourth year.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The time value of money and all cash flows after the payback period.

items.title: Accounting rate of return
items.core_explanation_md:
**ARR = average annual profit after tax and depreciation / investment x 100.**

**Two bases for investment:** the **initial investment**, or the **average investment = half of (initial investment - salvage value) + salvage value**.

ARR uses **accounting profit** (not cash flow) and **ignores the time value of money**, so two projects with the **same ARR** but different timing of benefits look alike.

variables.name: Mean profit after depreciation and tax

common_errors: Using cash inflow instead of profit

items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware notes an internal inconsistency: the numerator belongs to owners while the denominator is total investment.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Half of (initial investment less salvage value) plus salvage value.

items.title: Net present value
items.core_explanation_md:
**NPV = present value of net cash inflows - initial investment**, discounting each year's flow at the **required rate**.

**Decision:** **accept if NPV is positive**; **zero** means the project neither adds nor loses value; **negative** means reject. Among **mutually exclusive** projects, take the **higher NPV**.

**Working capital:** an **increase** is an **outflow**, a **decrease** an **inflow**. **EAC** compares assets with **different lives**.

variables.name: Net cash inflow in year t
Required rate of return (cost of capital)

assumptions: Cash flows occur at year ends
The discount rate is known and constant

items.expanded_explanation_md: NPV is the amount by which the value of the business rises if the project is undertaken.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a zero NPV mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The project earns exactly the required rate, adding neither value nor loss.

items.title: IRR and MIRR
items.core_explanation_md:
**IRR** is the discount rate at which **NPV = 0**. Find it by **trial and error**, then **interpolate**: lower rate + (NPV at lower rate / (NPV at lower + absolute NPV at higher)) x the gap between the rates. **Accept if IRR exceeds the cost of capital.**

**Limits:** **multiple IRRs** with **alternating cash flows**, and the assumption that inflows are **reinvested at the IRR**.

**MIRR** fixes this: **PVC** = present value of costs at the cost of capital; **TV** = inflows compounded to the end at the cost of capital; **MIRR solves PVC = TV / (1 + MIRR)^n**, giving **one** answer.

variables.name: Terminal value of inflows compounded at the cost of capital
Present value of costs at the cost of capital
Number of periods to the end of the project

assumptions: Inflows are reinvested at the cost of capital
Costs are financed at the cost of capital
common_errors: Compounding inflows at the IRR instead of the cost of capital
Using the number of cash flows instead of the number of periods

items.expanded_explanation_md: Both IRR and MIRR can mislead when ranking projects of different sizes, because a larger project with a lower rate can have the higher NPV.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can IRR give multiple answers?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When cash flows change sign more than once, the NPV equation can have several roots.

items.title: Profitability index and capital rationing
items.core_explanation_md:
**PI = sum of discounted cash inflows / initial cash outlay.**

**PI above 1** means profitable; **below 1** unprofitable. A **higher PI** ranks higher, even where another project has **larger absolute inflows**, because PI is **per rupee invested**.

**Capital rationing** limits the funds available; firms respond with norms such as a **higher IRR or PI hurdle**.

assumptions: Same discount rate for all projects
common_errors: Using NPV instead of present value of inflows in the numerator

items.expanded_explanation_md: PI above 1 is equivalent to a positive NPV for a given project.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can a project with the largest inflows have a low PI?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because its outlay is also very large, so inflow per rupee invested is low.

items.title: Social cost benefit analysis
items.core_explanation_md:
**SCBA** is used by **governments and local bodies** for **infrastructure** such as airports, ports and dams.

It gives **negative** value to **social costs** (pollution, loss of mangroves, health hazards) and **positive** value to **social benefits** (time and fuel savings, employment, better living standards).

The project is **beneficial** if the **net social result is positive** and at least equal to the project cost.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Unlike private appraisal, it counts costs and benefits to society, not only cash flows to the owner.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two social costs and two social benefits.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Costs: pollution and loss of mangroves. Benefits: time savings and employment.
